stem: A dataset of house prices has a mean of £500,000 and a median of £280,000. What does this tell you?

options.text: The data is normally distributed
Most houses cost around £500,000
The data is right-skewed — a few very expensive houses are pulling the mean up
The dataset has errors

explanation_after: When mean >> median, a few very high values are pulling the mean up (right skew). The median (£280,000) better represents the 'typical' house price here.

options.text: The middle value of a dataset
The most frequent value in a dataset
The average distance of values from the mean — how spread out the data is
The difference between the maximum and minimum values

explanation_after: Standard deviation measures spread around the mean. A high stdev means values are widely scattered; a low stdev means they cluster tightly around the mean.

stem: A correlation of 0.95 between variable X and Y means:

options.text: X causes Y
Changing X by 1 unit changes Y by 0.95 units
X and Y have a very strong positive linear relationship — they tend to increase together
95% of the variation in Y is explained by X

explanation_after: Correlation of 0.95 means a very strong positive linear relationship. It does NOT mean causation, and the 0.95 is NOT a slope (that's regression coefficient) or R² (that would be 0.90).

options.text: There is a 3% chance the null hypothesis is true
There is a 97% probability the alternative hypothesis is correct
If the null hypothesis were true, the probability of observing this data (or more extreme) is 3%
The effect size is 0.03

explanation_after: A p-value is P(data | H₀ is true). p=0.03 means: IF the null hypothesis were true, there's only 3% chance of seeing data this extreme. It does NOT give the probability that H₀ is true.

stem: You have two class score distributions, both with mean=75 but stdev A=5 and stdev B=20. What does this tell you?

options.text: Class A and B performed identically
Class A is more consistent — most students near 75; Class B has wide variance — many students far from 75
Class B has more students
Class A has higher outliers

explanation_after: Same mean, different spread. Class A (stdev=5) has tight clustering: ~68% of students score 70-80. Class B (stdev=20) has wide spread: many students scoring 55 or 95+. The mean alone is misleading.

stem: What is the main advantage of using the bootstrap method for confidence intervals?

options.text: It is always more accurate than parametric methods
It requires no assumptions about the data's distribution
It requires less data
It runs faster than analytical methods

explanation_after: Bootstrap resampling makes no assumptions about the underlying distribution. It works for any statistic (mean, median, correlation) even when the data is not normally distributed.

stem: Before training many ML models, features are standardised using z = (x − mean) / std. Why is this step important when features have very different scales, e.g. 'age' (0–100) and 'income' (0–200,000)?

options.text: It makes the data look nicer in plots but doesn't affect training
Without it, features with larger raw ranges (like income) can dominate distance-based or gradient-based calculations, even if they're not more informative
It removes outliers automatically
It converts categorical features into numbers

explanation_after: Standardisation rescales each feature to mean 0, std 1. Without it, a feature like income (range in the hundreds of thousands) can dwarf a feature like age (range 0–100) in distance calculations (k-NN, clustering) or gradient magnitudes (gradient descent), causing the model to implicitly overweight large-scale features regardless of their actual importance.

stem: You test Model A (91.2% accuracy) against Model B (91.6% accuracy) on the same test set, and a statistical significance test gives p = 0.41 for the difference. What is the correct conclusion?

options.text: Model B is definitely better because 91.6 > 91.2
The observed difference is small enough that it could easily arise from random chance — there isn't strong evidence Model B is actually better
The models are 41% similar
You need to retrain Model A

explanation_after: A high p-value (0.41, far above typical thresholds like 0.05) means that if the two models were truly equally good, a difference this size would be unsurprising due to random sampling in the test set. A small accuracy bump alone doesn't prove one model is genuinely better — this is why rigorous ML evaluation uses significance testing, not just raw metric comparison.
